1	// SPDX-License-Identifier: CC0-1.0

3	//! Engine state for the com-amazonaws-sqs-amazonsqs service.
4	//!
5	//! The queue is this service's primary resource: `CreateQueue` allocates one,
6	//! `GetQueueUrl` resolves it by name, `GetQueueAttributes` reports it,
7	//! `SetQueueAttributes` changes it and `DeleteQueue` removes it, all against the SAME
8	//! [`Queue`] record in [`ComAmazonawsSqsAmazonsqsState::queues`], so a create is
9	//! observable by every later read and an attribute change by every later report.
10	//!
11	//! # One namespace per region
12	//!
13	//! A queue belongs to the region the call that created it addressed ([`Queue::region`],
14	//! taken from the request's SigV4 credential scope by [`request_region`]), and the store
15	//! is keyed by that region together with the queue's name: a queue name "is unique within
16	//! the scope of your queues" of one region, so the same name created against a second
17	//! region is a second, independent queue and each delivers only its own messages.
18	//! Everything that resolves a queue takes that region —
19	//! [`ComAmazonawsSqsAmazonsqsState::queue`], [`ComAmazonawsSqsAmazonsqsState::queue_mut`],
20	//! [`ComAmazonawsSqsAmazonsqsState::queue_by_url`] and
21	//! [`ComAmazonawsSqsAmazonsqsState::queues_in`] — so a call signed for one region resolves
22	//! nothing another region holds, and the region the queue lives in is the one its ARN
23	//! carries ([`queue_arn`]). An ARN a request supplies is read the same way
24	//! ([`parse_queue_arn`]): one naming another region names no queue here, which is why
25	//! neither a dead-letter target nor a message movement task can span two regions.
26	//!
27	//! The record is the stored half; the wire half (the `Attributes` map
28	//! `GetQueueAttributes` returns) is PROJECTED from it by
29	//! [`Queue::reported_attributes`], so no handler assembles a response member by hand.
30	//! Server-side encryption is part of that projection: which of the two mutually
31	//! exclusive options a queue is on, and what it therefore reports, lives in
32	//! [`encryption`], as does the KMS permission a call that uses the queue's key needs.
33	//!
34	//! # The message plane
35	//!
36	//! A queue also HOLDS its messages: [`Queue::messages`] is the arrival-order deque
37	//! `SendMessage` appends to and `ReceiveMessage` hands out of, and [`Queue::handles`]
38	//! maps the receipt handle a receive minted to the message it names, which is what
39	//! `DeleteMessage` resolves — and [`Queue::deleted_handles`] remembers the handles a
40	//! delete has already consumed, so repeating a delete that succeeded is idempotent
41	//! rather than refused. HANDING a message over is [`Queue::hand_over`], the one path
42	//! every consumer of a queue takes — this service's own `ReceiveMessage` and a poller
43	//! another service runs over the same queue — so what one delivery does to a message's
44	//! counts, its visibility and its receipt handle is stated once. A handle is not an opaque
45	//! value with no provenance: it carries
46	//! the queue incarnation that minted it ([`Queue::mint_receipt_handle`]), so
47	//! [`ComAmazonawsSqsAmazonsqsState::receipt_handle_origin`] can tell this queue's own
48	//! handle from one another queue issued and from one a deleted incarnation issued, which
49	//! are three refusals a caller recovers from differently. Visibility and retention are
50	//! evaluated against the clock
51	//! by [`Queue::materialise_due`], so the three `ApproximateNumberOfMessages*`
52	//! attributes are counts over real state rather than made-up values. A message carries
53	//! the visibility timeout it was RECEIVED under, so a later change to the queue's
54	//! attribute spares it, while a FIFO queue's delay is re-derived from the queue's
55	//! current value by [`Queue::reapply_delay_seconds`], which is where the
56	//! FIFO-versus-standard retroactivity of `DelaySeconds` lives.
57	//!
58	//! Which of those messages a receive may hand over is [`Queue::delivery_order`]: on a
59	//! standard queue whatever is visible, and on a FIFO queue each message group in strict
60	//! send order, one group member in flight at a time. A FIFO send also remembers the
61	//! deduplication token it accepted a message under, in [`Queue::deduplication`], so a
62	//! resend inside the interval is accepted without delivering a second copy, and
63	//! sequences the message from [`Queue::sequenced`].
64	//!
65	//! A FIFO RECEIVE is idempotent the same way: the batch it handed over under a
66	//! `ReceiveRequestAttemptId` is remembered in [`Queue::receive_attempts`], so a retry
67	//! carrying that same token hands the identical messages and receipt handles back
68	//! instead of a second, different batch.
69	//!
70	//! `PurgeQueue` empties that plane through [`Queue::purge`]: the messages, the receipt
71	//! handles naming them, the remembered receive attempts that named them and the
72	//! deduplication tokens that would suppress a resend all go, and the instant of the
73	//! purge is remembered, so a further purge inside [`PURGE_QUEUE_INTERVAL`] of it is
74	//! refused ([`Queue::purge_in_progress`]).
75	//!
76	//! # Dead-letter redrive
77	//!
78	//! A queue whose `RedrivePolicy` names a dead-letter target only lets a message be

I split the 4,877-line `state.rs` into focused modules and removed one duplicated snippet. Behavior is unchanged. Tests pass (280 integration plus 5 unit, 0 failures), and `cargo clippy --all-targets` shows no warnings for this crate.

`state.rs` is now 1,241 lines. It holds limits, wording helpers and module wiring, and re-exports the new modules, so no caller or test path changed. Each move is its own commit with the reason in the message.

| Commit | What moved |
|---|---|
| 9b7a26dc7 | `queue_address`: queue key, ARN and URL helpers |
| 45e82ef7c | `receipt_handle`: handle format, origin and refusal wording |
| 76625f120 | `clock`: epoch renderings and seconds/after/lapsed |
| e7f48a2d0 | `message_digest`: message ids, MD5s and the dedup token |
| 15e1892af | `message_move_task`: the task record, schedule and wording |
| 2fd61bc47 | `queue_tags`: tag limits and refusals |
| c225704a7 | `queue_attributes`: the settable-attribute table and its validation |
| bd3b99d23 | `queue`: `Queue`, `StoredMessage` and the delivery types |
| d39e3f236 | `store`: the store struct and its operations |
| 4e876f7e4 | `Queue::authorization_subject()` replaces the same owned (ARN, policy) pair built in 18 handlers |
| 86fd13b2d | README layout section updated |

- **Visibility:** the code was moved as is. Five private items became `pub(super)` because `state.rs` still uses them. They are `queue_arn_fields`, `encoded_opaque_token`, `RECEIPT_HANDLE_FIELD_SEPARATOR`, `epoch_seconds` and three `MessageMoveTask` methods.
- **Commit scope:** the message-move commit (15e1892af) also re-wraps the module doc comments from the earlier moves. That is a small departure from one kind of change per commit.
- **Imports:** the new modules use `use super::*;`, which matches the existing `permissions`, `redrive` and `message_attributes` modules. Explicit import lists would be tidier, but they would be a different convention from the crate's own.
- **Left alone:**
  - The `#[allow(unused_imports)]` lines in `ops/`, which sit on generated scaffold code.
  - The `.expect(...)` calls, which carry real invariants.
  - Existing em dashes in comments, because rewording them would bury the moves.
  - The crate-wide rustfmt drift (generated code, not touched).

The wording-helper constants and builders in `state.rs` are the next obvious split, and the `ops/` handlers share more boilerplate. Both are worth doing as separate passes if you want to go further.
